posts:
Financial anxiety clashes with relentless consumer spending as commentators blame lattes while households drown in debt.
Evidence: Stated Personal Waste, Actual Systemic Debt, Actual Personal Strain
#Economy #Aletheia 🌐

Commentators claim Americans' financial struggles stem purely from poor lifestyle choices, social media comparison, and undisciplined luxury spending like lattes and new phones.
Stated Judgement: (+0.50, +0.50) — Greater Good

Rising household debt and sticky inflation force families to rely on credit and buy-now-pay-later schemes just to maintain basic living standards amidst soaring costs.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.60, -0.70) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Destruction.

Integrity: Partially Distorted (Hypocrisy: 4.50, Uncertainty z: 2)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Ted Jenkin Commentary: COND (0.5, 0.5) — Blames psychology over macro costs.
- Consumer Debt Reality: PASS (-0.6, -0.7) — Highlights real debt and financing traps.
Amidst reports that nearly half of Americans feel broke despite rising headline spending, commentators debate whether personal choices or macroeconomic pressures drive the crisis.

The Poison:
Using individual consumer habits as a scapegoat deflects accountability from structural inflation, stagnant wages, and predatory financing models.
This analysis commits a Metaphysical error by confusing individual consumer coping mechanisms with the primary structural drivers of household financial insecurity.

Social Physics Analysis:
Commentators deploy a smart selfish maneuver: substituting systemic economic strain with moralizing projections about social media vanity to protect existing economic frameworks.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When you map the gap between moralizing pretexts and structural debt, it plots a trajectory toward Lesser Evil, where systemic failure is rebranded as personal vice.

The Unavoidable Truth: Easy financing and lifestyle inflation mask profound underlying financial insecurity.
The Unavoidable Lie: Consumer spending proves everyone is wealthy.

Alethekanon:
Moralizing about lattes while ignoring systemic wage stagnation is a transparent deflection. True financial health requires structural reform, not lifestyle shaming.

Awwthekanon:
People aren't drowning in debt because they buy lattes; they're trying to keep their heads above water in a punishing economy. Let's have some real empathy.

Brothekanon:
Come on man, blaming a $5 coffee for someone being broke when rent doubled is wild. People are just trying to survive out here.

Spirithekanon:
"Woe to those who add house to house and join field to field" Isaiah 5:8 PASS
Blaming the vulnerable for structural extraction blinds society to the true cost of systemic greed.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Americans say they're broke. So why can't they stop spending so much?

Consumer confidence is in the basement, yet consumer spending keeps rising. A financial expert reveals five essential reasons behind the disconnect.

Actual Article Body:

Market data provided by Factset. Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions. Legal Statement. Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG.

Will Cain breaks down the economic track record on inflation and housing prices under the Trump and Biden administrations ahead of the midterms.

Some Americans are crying poverty with a $1,500 iPhone in one hand and an $8 Starbucks latte in the other. They say groceries are unaffordable, but somehow the restaurants are packed, airports are crowded, and the neighbor just pulled into his driveway with a brand-new $90,000 SUV.

Apparently, we're one bad economic report away from bankruptcy and one Instagram post away from booking another trip to Cabo.

Consumer confidence is in the basement. Consumer spending apparently didn't get the memo.

US ECONOMY NOTCHES REMARKABLE NEW RECORD, SPARKING CHEERS: ‘GOOD JOB EVERYONE’

In September, the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index fell to 81.9. Yet it has been reported that consumer credit and debit card spending per household increased 6.2% from a year earlier.

Consumer confidence is down, but consumer spending is up. (iStock)

So, what's going on?

IT’S NOT THE ECONOMY, STUPID. AMERICANS VOTE BASED ON THEIR PERSONAL ECONOMY

As a financial advisor, I think the answer involves something more powerful than inflation or interest rates. Human psychology.

And there are five reasons our spending habits aren't matching our economic anxiety.

WE ALL ARE DESPERATE FOR A FINANCIAL CHECK-UP. TIME TO SAY, ‘SHOW ME THE MONEY!’

Thirty years ago, you compared your lifestyle with the neighbor who bought a new Cadillac.

Today, you're comparing yourself with 5,000 people on Instagram. There are even college degrees on how to become a social media influencer. None of them get lots of likes by telling you to eat ramen noodles and skip third-row seats for the latest rock concert.

Someone's vacationing in Italy. Someone remodeled their kitchen. Someone bought a new Porsche. Face it. Someone is always doing better than you are. Or, it seems that way.

You're comparing your everyday financial reality with everybody else's highlight reel. Social media has turned keeping up with the Joneses into keeping up with the Kardashians.

Except the Kardashians can actually afford it.

3 BIG QUESTIONS TO ASK MOM AND DAD BEFORE YOU MAKE A MAJOR FINANCIAL COMMITMENT

Remember when people saved money before buying something? It’s called layaway. Today, almost anything can be financed.

SKIP TWO YEARS OF COLLEGE DEBT AND GIVE YOUR FAMILY A LIFETIME OF WEALTH

That $1,200 purchase? Just four easy payments of $300. The vacation? Monthly installments. The furniture? Zero down.

Apparently, we're one bad economic report away from bankruptcy and one Instagram post away from booking another trip to Cabo.

We've become experts at making expensive things look cheap by dividing them into smaller payments.

GEN Z IS WORKING HARD, BUT THE ECONOMY IS PUTTING THE AMERICAN DREAM OUT OF REACH FOR MANY

The problem isn't necessarily buy now, pay later. It's forgetting how many things you've already agreed to pay for later. And eventually, later shows up.

Not everybody spending money is financially struggling.

Higher-income Americans with substantial investment portfolios have benefited from rising asset prices. Many can comfortably afford expensive vacations and new cars.

Meanwhile, other households are stretching their paychecks just to maintain their lifestyles. Some spending growth also reflects higher prices for necessities.

The economy isn't treating every consumer equally. When you see your neighbor's new Mercedes, you don't know whether he paid cash or financed it for 84 months.

You see the car. Not the car payment.

When people worry about the future, they don't always save more. Sometimes they spend more.

Had a terrible week? Amazon makes it your birthday every day. Stressed about work? Book a vacation. Worried about the economy? Just get a good meal out at a local restaurant.

Retail therapy is a lot more fun than retirement planning. Unfortunately, the happiness from that purchase may disappear long before the credit card bill does.

Americans have become obsessed with displaying wealth rather than accumulating it. The luxury car. The designer handbag. The vacation pictures.

But here's something I've learned after decades of advising families. Net worth doesn't have an Instagram account.

I've met millionaires who drive 10-year-old cars and people earning $250,000 who couldn't cover a $10,000 emergency. Income isn't wealth. And spending certainly isn't wealth.

You're comparing your everyday financial reality with everybody else's highlight reel. Social media has turned keeping up with the Joneses into keeping up with the Kardashians.

Why? Because I wrote the book. So, before you swear off Starbucks forever, try three simple changes.

First, put every nonessential purchase over $100 on a 48-hour waiting list or online cart. If you still want it two days later and can afford it, buy it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Second, take buy now, pay later off the menu for 30 days. If you can't pay cash for a discretionary purchase, you probably shouldn't be buying it.

Third, automatically move 5% of every paycheck into savings before you spend a dime. Start smaller if your budget can't handle 5%. The point is to pay yourself before you pay everybody else. Not the other way around.

This isn't about living like a monk. It's about remembering who's in charge of your money.

I'm not suggesting Americans should stop enjoying their money. Life is meant to be lived. But there's a difference between enjoying your money and spending it to impress people who aren't paying your bills.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Your neighbor's new car isn't proof he's winning financially. It might just mean he's winning the monthly-payment contest.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM TED JENKIN

Do Americans own the president's papers? Appeals court to weigh in

The administration says papers created in the White House belong to Donald Trump, not to the American people. The case could ultimately end up at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court.

Actual Article Body:
Carrie Johnson

A flag featuring Donald Trump waves amid a group of supporters near Mar-a-Lago, Fla., in 2024.
                
                    
                    Alon Skuy/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

President Trump has famously pushed the bounds of executive power since he returned to the White House. In arguments Friday before a federal appeals court in Washington, administration lawyers will make an especially bold claim: that papers created in the White House belong to Donald Trump, not to the American people. The move comes amid a series of actions under Trump's second term to test the limits put in place after the Watergate scandal, and could be another case that ends up at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court.

Six months ago, the Justice Department moved to invalidate the Presidential Records Act, a federal law in place since 1978. Conservative lawyer Michael Edney cast the move in a long line of other attempts to pare back statutes from that era.

"This is a story about a post-Watergate, overbroad statutory incursion into the prerogatives of the executive branch," Edney said in a recent webinar sponsored by the Federalist Society.

For some 200 years, presidents could decide for themselves what to do with the papers they created in office, until disputes with Richard Nixon prompted Congress to weigh in. Every president since then has complied with the records law, until this year.

"The Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional and a clear violation of the separation of powers," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.

The White House's reinterpretation of the act comes after Trump was indicted on obstruction of justice charges for allegedly stockpiling classified documents in a bathroom, ballroom and office at his Mar-a-Lago resort. A federal judge threw out the case for technical reasons, related to the appointment of the prosecutor, and the Justice Department ultimately dropped the case after Trump won reelection.

Nikhel Sus is chief counsel for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a watchdog group that sued over the Trump move.

"If the courts were to accept it, and we are hopeful that they will not, it would mean the people really have no right of access to the president's papers and that would be a major loss for archivists, historians and to the American people writ large," Sus said.

Senior U.S. District Judge John Bates, an appointee of former President George W. Bush, ruled against the Trump White House this year, in a decision that opened with a passage from George Orwell's dystopian novel 1984: "Who controls the past controls the future; who controls the present controls the past," the judge wrote.

Three judges from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit will consider the issue on Friday.

The Trump administration said in court papers that keeping all those records imposes a burden on the White House and that it could chill advisers from having honest conversations with the president.

But former government officials say being able to consult these papers is essential.

"Access to the records on national security issues of former presidents is really vital for the continuity of our government," said John Bellinger, who served as legal adviser to the National Security Council under George W. Bush.

Bellinger said he and other members of Bush's staff sometimes requested the papers of President Bill Clinton, to understand conversations Clinton had with world leaders and members of Congress.

"Often the only record of what a president has said to a foreign leader — or perhaps even more important, what a foreign leader, friend or foe, has said to the president of the United States — is in a written document," Bellinger said.

To not be able to see those papers, he said, will leave future presidents at a "terrible disadvantage."

Edney, who also worked for Bush's National Security Council and Justice Department, said he believed that Congress could probably pass a "thoughtful" records preservation statute. He said parts of the current Presidential Records Act that provide Congress with automatic access and presume the records will be publicly disclosed are "constitutionally problematic."

Edney said he has some doubts about whether the watchdog groups suing to challenge Trump's move actually have legal standing to proceed.

But the Trump administration appears to have breezed past those concerns, because they have a higher goal in mind.

"They want this to go to the Supreme Court," Edney said. "I think they want this resolved at a time of their choosing, with arguments of their choosing, and a court of their choosing, and with the Solicitor General's office that's making their arguments, as opposed to a subsequent administration."
